1200	There is something very good
1201	in this,
1202	that it is outside of itself.
1203	One who has mochin,
1204	is in devekut, because he is bound
1205	to...
1206	he is bound to the truth that he grasps.
1207	His mochin.
1208	He is attached.
1209	Someone who is outwardly directed, that is toward the other.
1210	The other can also be HaShem, if he loves HaShem.
1211	It says there is someone who loves.
1212	And how does it develop, that there is someone who loves?
1213	When all the time he is also thinking about himself.
1214	Where am I?
1215	How much do I love?
1216	Yesterday perhaps I loved more, perhaps...
1217	I fell. After all, it says "a tzaddik falls seven times," and here.
1218	Where is this "falls seven times"?
1219	In the midot, the seven midot.
1220	Since the midot are being affected, I am affected, so there is also a lot of thinking about myself.
1221	Is this good or not good?
1222	It is not good.
1223	It is a bad thing.
1224	Therefore it is written that the midot, thinking about oneself, is called the Tree of Knowledge of good
1225	and evil.
1226	That is its root; it is called bad self-awareness.
1227	Now, I can say even more outward.
1228	So here he writes that malchut is a leap outward.
1229	But what can be good in this?
1230	That since someone who is truly a king, who has the quality of kingship, is so
1231	much outside of himself, he is also bound to the service
1232	of his own, so that he does not think about himself either.
1233	What is this like?
1234	There is a man who has aches; one day a noise in his head, a noise in his belly,
1235	in his hand, in his leg.
1236	A sign that it is not from the outside.
1237	If he were a king, he would be so outside of himself,
1238	that he has no time; he cannot think about himself
1239	at all.
